pos: n. (the treasurer and scribe of Hezekiah's court, denounced by Isaiah for hewing himself a sepulchre on high and deposed from his stewardship)
etymology: From Hebrew Shebna or Shebnah, probably from a root meaning vigour or youthfulness. The Authorized Version calls him treasurer at Isaiah 22:15 and scribe at 2 Kings 18:18 — the same man in two stations, the second lower than the first.
biblical_def: Shebna is the court official of Hezekiah's reign whom the LORD singled out by name for judgment, and the only steward in Scripture whose deposition is prophesied in advance and then quietly recorded as accomplished. Isaiah is sent to him with a stinging errand: “Go, get thee unto this treasurer, even unto Shebna, which is over the house” (Isa 22:15). The charge is not embezzlement or treason but a monument. “What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here, that thou hast hewed thee out a sepulchre here” (Isa 22:16) — a foreigner by every indication, with no father named and no inheritance in the land, cutting himself a rock-tomb among the graves of Judah's great men so that the nation would have to remember him. The sentence is stated plainly: “I will drive thee from thy station, and from thy state shall he pull thee down” (Isa 22:19), and the office is handed to another: “I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah” (Isa 22:20). By the time Sennacherib's army stands at the conduit, the transfer has happened. Eliakim is “over the household” and Shebna is merely “the scribe” (2Ki 18:18). He is still useful, still trusted enough to be sent to Isaiah in sackcloth (2Ki 19:2), but he is no longer over the house. God demoted him and then kept him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Shebna; in sacred history he is Hezekiah's treasurer, deposed from the stewardship of the house and left as scribe.
webster_full: SHEBNA, n. An officer of the court of Hezekiah king of Judah.
He was over the house, that is, steward or comptroller of the royal household.
Isaiah was sent to reprove him for hewing out a sepulchre for himself in the rock.
His station was given to Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, and he was made scribe.
In that lower office he was sent with Eliakim to the prophet in the year of Sennacherib.
scriptures: Thus saith the Lord GOD of hosts, Go, get thee unto this treasurer, even unto Shebna, which is over the house, and say,
What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here, that thou hast hewed thee out a sepulchre here, as he that heweth him out a sepulchre on high, and that graveth an habitation for himself in a rock?
And I will drive thee from thy station, and from thy state shall he pull thee down.

And I will clothe him with thy robe, and strengthen him with thy girdle, and I will commit thy government into his hand: and he shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to the house of Judah.
corruption_summary: The modern misuse is to read Shebna's fall as a lesson in personal branding gone wrong. Scripture reads it as the LORD's judgment on a steward who used a trust to build a name, and as the occasion for a promise that reaches past Eliakim to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Shebna is handled today, when he is handled at all, as a cautionary tale about ego in leadership — a management failure with a spiritual veneer. That reading empties the oracle. Isaiah does not tell Shebna he has damaged his effectiveness; he tells him the LORD will drive him from his station. The sin named is not poor self-awareness but the theft of a stewardship: a man set over another man's house who spent the house's resources carving his own memorial into it. That is the standing temptation of every officer of the church, and Scripture treats it as a matter for divine sentence, not for coaching.

The passage also carries a promise the pulpit must not surrender to management-speak. Of Eliakim the LORD says, “the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open” (Isa 22:22), and the risen Christ takes those very words for Himself: “he that hath the key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth” (Rev 3:7). Even Eliakim, the better steward, is warned that the nail in the sure place will one day be cut down (Isa 22:25). Every human steward is temporary; only One holds the key by right. Shebna's tomb is the monument of a servant who forgot he was one.
roots_summary: Hebrew Shebna (H7644), Shebna; sokén (H5532), treasurer, steward; bayith (H1004), house, household; qeber (H6913), grave, sepulchre; maddaph — see rather hadaph (H1920), to thrust or drive out.

Hebrew sokén (H5532) — treasurer, steward; the office Isaiah names in the summons.
Hebrew bayith (H1004) — house; ‘over the house’ is the technical title of the chief officer.
Hebrew qeber (H6913) — grave, sepulchre; the monument Shebna hewed for himself.
Hebrew hadaph (H1920) — to thrust away, drive out; the verb of his deposition.
usage: “Go, get thee unto this treasurer” — the LORD sends a prophet to one bureaucrat by name.
“What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here?” — a man with no roots buying himself a monument.
“And Shebna the scribe” — the demotion recorded without comment, four chapters later.

pos: n. (a prince of Judah under Jehoiakim, son of Achbor, who fetched the prophet Urijah out of Egypt to his death and afterward pleaded with the king not to burn the scroll of Jeremiah)
etymology: From Hebrew Elnathan, compounded of El, God, and nathan, he gave — God hath given. The same name is borne by three of Ezra's messengers to Casiphia and by the grandfather of Jehoiachin.
biblical_def: Elnathan the son of Achbor is one of the most instructive minor figures in the closing years of Judah, because Scripture shows him doing an evil thing and a right thing within ten chapters, and never resolves the man into a type. He first appears as the king's agent in an extradition: “And Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt, namely, Elnathan the son of Achbor, and certain men with him into Egypt” (Jer 26:22). The errand was to recover the prophet Urijah, who had fled for preaching what Jeremiah preached, and its end is stated without softening: they “fetched forth Urijah out of Egypt, and brought him unto Jehoiakim the king; who slew him with the sword” (Jer 26:23). Elnathan carried a faithful prophet home to be murdered. Yet when Jehoiakim sat in his winterhouse cutting Jeremiah's roll with a penknife and casting it in the fire, Elnathan is one of three men who spoke: “Nevertheless Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the roll: but he would not hear them” (Jer 36:25). He sat among the princes in the scribe's chamber when the roll was read (Jer 36:12), and something in the reading moved him. He is very probably the Elnathan of Jerusalem whose daughter Nehushta was the mother of Jehoiachin (2Ki 24:8), which makes him grandfather to a king. Scripture leaves him there: a man who did the state's dirty work and then risked the state's displeasure, and whose end is not recorded.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Elnathan; in sacred history he is a prince of Jehoiakim's court, son of Achbor, sent into Egypt after the prophet Urijah.
webster_full: ELNATHAN, n. God hath given; a proper name of several men in the Hebrew Scriptures.
Chiefly, a prince in the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah, the son of Achbor.
He was sent into Egypt to bring back the prophet Urijah, who was there slain by the king.
He was among the princes who heard the roll of Jeremiah read in the scribe's chamber.
Three men of the name were sent by Ezra to Casiphia to obtain ministers for the house of God.
scriptures: And Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt, namely, Elnathan the son of Achbor, and certain men with him into Egypt.

Then he went down into the king's house, into the scribe's chamber: and, lo, all the princes sat there, even Elishama the scribe, and Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, and Elnathan the son of Achbor, and Gemariah the son of Shaphan, and Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the princes.
Nevertheless Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the roll: but he would not hear them.
Ezr 8:16

Then sent I for Eliezer, for Ariel, for Shemaiah, and for Elnathan, and for Jarib, and for Elnathan, and for Nathan, and for Zechariah, and for Meshullam, chief men; also for Joiarib, and for Elnathan, men of understanding.
corruption_summary: The modern instinct is to grade Elnathan on balance — a decent man in a bad job. Scripture neither excuses the extradition nor cancels the intercession, and thereby refuses the accounting altogether.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic reading of Elnathan is that he was conflicted, that he did what he had to do, and that his later protest shows his heart was in the right place. Scripture will not have it. Urijah is dead, and Elnathan fetched him. The intercession over the roll does not undo that; it is simply the next thing he did, and it was right. Both facts stand in the record with no verdict attached, and the effect is to strip away the arithmetic by which men reckon themselves acceptable — the ledger of good outweighing bad which is the natural religion of every fallen heart and the flat contradiction of justification by faith alone.

What the passage does teach plainly is the impotence of private conscience inside public complicity. Three princes pleaded, “but he would not hear them” (Jer 36:25), and the roll burned anyway. A man in office who has already lent his hands to one injustice has spent the moral weight he would need for the next. The Reformed doctrine of the lesser magistrate is precisely the answer Elnathan did not give: an officer under an unrighteous command is not a neutral instrument, and the time to refuse is the first errand, not the second.

Hebrew El (H410) — God; the theophoric element opening the name.
Hebrew nathan (H5414) — to give, bestow; the verb closing it.
Hebrew sar (H8269) — prince, chief, official; his rank in the scribe's chamber.

“Had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the roll” — the protest that came too late to matter.
“For Elnathan… men of understanding” — the name borne later by better men in Ezra's train.

pos: n. (an officer of Josiah sent to enquire of the LORD at the finding of the book of the law; also an Edomite king's father in the generations of Esau)
etymology: From Hebrew Akbor, a mouse or field-mouse — one of the many Hebrew names drawn from the creatures, like Deborah the bee, Jonah the dove, and Caleb the dog. Second Chronicles 34:20 gives the same officer as Abdon the son of Micah.
biblical_def: Achbor the son of Michaiah stands in the small company of men whom Josiah sent when the book of the law was found in the house of the LORD and the king rent his clothes. The commission is recorded by name: “the king commanded Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam the son of Shaphan, and Achbor the son of Michaiah, and Shaphan the scribe, and Asahiah a servant of the king's” (2Ki 22:12). Five men — a high priest, two officials, a scribe and a royal servant — and their errand was not to convene a council but to find out what God meant to do. They went to a woman: “So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asahiah, went unto Huldah the prophetess” (2Ki 22:14), and her answer set the shape of Josiah's whole reformation. Achbor is named nowhere in the reform itself; he appears once more only as the father of Elnathan, the prince who fetched Urijah from Egypt for Jehoiakim (Jer 26:22). The name belongs also to an Edomite: “Baalhanan the son of Achbor reigned in his stead” (Gen 36:38), in the line of dukes who ruled in Edom before any king reigned over Israel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Achbor; in sacred history he is one of the five officers Josiah sent to Huldah when the book of the law was found.
webster_full: ACHBOR, n. A mouse; a proper name in the Hebrew Scriptures.
One of the officers whom Josiah sent to enquire of the LORD concerning the book found in the temple.
He is called Abdon the son of Micah in the parallel place of the Chronicles.
He was the father of Elnathan, a prince in the court of Jehoiakim.
Also, the father of Baalhanan, one of the kings who reigned in the land of Edom.
scriptures: And the king commanded Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam the son of Shaphan, and Achbor the son of Michaiah, and Shaphan the scribe, and Asahiah a servant of the king's, saying,

So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asahiah, went unto Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college;) and they communed with her.
And Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt, namely, Elnathan the son of Achbor, and certain men with him into Egypt.
And Saul died, and Baalhanan the son of Achbor reigned in his stead.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that the right response to the recovered word of God is dread and enquiry, not administration.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Achbor is a name in a list and nobody has contested him. What his errand sets against the modern church is the behaviour of men who find the Bible after a long institutional silence. Josiah's officers did not appoint a committee, commission a study, or negotiate an implementation timetable. The king tore his clothes and sent five of his most senior men out of the palace to ask a prophetess what the LORD intended to do to them, because the book they had just heard read pronounced curses they knew they had earned.

The principle to recover is that Scripture is a word from God about God's intentions toward the hearer, and the first sane reaction to reading it is fear. Huldah's reply confirmed the curse and only then granted Josiah a delay for the tenderness of his heart. The modern habit of receiving the Bible as a resource to be consulted rather than a sentence to be answered would have been unintelligible to the five men walking to the college quarter of Jerusalem that morning. Achbor is remembered because he went.

usage: “Achbor the son of Michaiah” — one of five men sent out at the finding of the book.
“Went unto Huldah the prophetess” — the errand of a court that had learned to fear.
“Elnathan the son of Achbor” — a faithful father and a compromised son.

pos: n. (the Pharisee and doctor of the law who counselled the council to let the apostles alone, and at whose feet Saul of Tarsus was brought up)
etymology: From Hebrew Gamli'el, reward of God or God is my recompense, from gamal, to deal out or requite, and El, God. The prince of Manasseh in the wilderness census bears the same name (Num 1:10); the Pharisee of Acts is a different man of a much later age.
biblical_def: Gamaliel is introduced at the moment the Sanhedrin has resolved to kill the apostles: “Then stood there up one in the council, a Pharisee, named Gamaliel, a doctor of the law, had in reputation among all the people” (Act 5:34). His speech is the most famous piece of pragmatism in the New Testament. He recites two failed messianic risings, Theudas and Judas of Galilee, and draws his conclusion: “Refrain from these men, and let them alone: for if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought” (Act 5:38), “But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God” (Act 5:39). The council took the advice as far as it suited them: “when they had called the apostles, and beaten them, they commanded that they should not speak in the name of Jesus” (Act 5:40). Gamaliel appears once more, in Paul's own mouth on the stairs of the castle: “brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers” (Act 22:3). He was therefore the teacher of the man who would carry the gospel to the Gentiles, and he taught him nothing that saved him. Saul went out from Gamaliel's feet to hold the coats of the men stoning Stephen, and it took Christ on the Damascus road to undo the education.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Gamaliel; in sacred history he is a Pharisee and teacher of the law in the council at Jerusalem, and the master under whom Saul of Tarsus was trained.
webster_full: GAMALIEL, n. Reward of God; a proper name in the Hebrew and Greek Scriptures.
A Pharisee and doctor of the law, held in reputation among all the people.
He counselled the council at Jerusalem to refrain from the apostles and let them alone.
Saul of Tarsus, afterwards the apostle Paul, was brought up at his feet.
Also, the son of Pedahzur, prince of the tribe of Manasseh in the wilderness.
scriptures: Act 5:34
Then stood there up one in the council, a Pharisee, named Gamaliel, a doctor of the law, had in reputation among all the people, and commanded to put the apostles forth a little space;
Act 5:38
And now I say unto you, Refrain from these men, and let them alone: for if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought:
Act 5:39
But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God.
Act 22:3

I am verily a man which am a Jew, born in Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, yet brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers, and was zealous toward God, as ye all are this day.
corruption_summary: Gamaliel's counsel is quoted today as a rule of Christian tolerance — leave every movement alone and let history sort it. Luke records the speech as the reasoning of an unconverted man, and Scripture elsewhere commands the church to judge doctrine now, not to wait and see.
corruption_paragraphs: “If it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it” is one of the most abused sentences in the Bible. It is preached as a maxim of broad-mindedness and used to silence anyone who tests a teaching or names an error: let it alone, and if God is not in it, it will collapse. But Luke is not endorsing the speech; he is reporting what a respected rabbi said in a council that then beat the apostles anyway. Success is not a mark of truth. Islam did not come to nought. The papacy did not come to nought. Endurance proves persistence, not divine origin, and a rule that treats duration as vindication would have to justify every long-lived error in the history of the world.

Scripture commands the opposite posture. The Bereans searched the scriptures daily to see whether the things Paul preached were so (Act 17:11); John commands, “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world” (1Jn 4:1); Paul charges Titus with elders able “by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9). Gamaliel's neutrality was not wisdom but unbelief with good manners — a man who could not decide whether the resurrection had happened, standing in the same room as men who had seen it. And the fruit of his school is the plainest argument against him: the finest theological education in Judaism produced a persecutor, and grace, not tuition, made him an apostle.

Greek nomodidaskalos (G3547) — doctor of the law; the title Luke gives him.
Greek Pharisaios (G5330) — Pharisee; the party to which he belonged.

“Refrain from these men, and let them alone” — neutrality offered as counsel.
“At the feet of Gamaliel” — the best education in Israel, and it saved no one.

pos: n. (the captain of Nebuchadnezzar's guard charged with slaying the wise men of Babylon, who brought Daniel before the king; also a king of Ellasar in the confederacy of Chedorlaomer)
etymology: From Hebrew and Aramaic Aryok, probably from a root meaning lion-like, and by some traced to an Elamite or Hurrian original. Two men of the name stand a thousand years apart in the record, and Scripture keeps them distinct by their offices rather than their spelling.
biblical_def: Arioch is the officer through whom the whole crisis of Daniel 2 is turned. Nebuchadnezzar, tormented by a dream his magicians could neither recall nor read, “was angry and very furious, and commanded to destroy all the wise men of Babylon” (Dan 2:12), and the sentence swept up four Hebrew captives who had never been consulted: “they sought Daniel and his fellows to be slain” (Dan 2:13). Into that came the executioner. “Then Daniel answered with counsel and wisdom to Arioch the captain of the king's guard, which was gone forth to slay the wise men of Babylon” (Dan 2:14). The Authorized Version's counsel and wisdom renders a phrase meaning prudence and discretion; Daniel did not resist and did not plead, but asked a question — “Why is the decree so hasty from the king?” — and the captain answered him. Arioch then does two more things: he grants the delay, and when Daniel returns with the secret he takes him to the throne room himself, “in haste” (Dan 2:25), with a courtier's eagerness to be the man who found the solution. He is a pagan soldier doing his duty, and God used his willingness to stop and listen to spare the lives of every wise man in Babylon. The older Arioch is king of Ellasar in the four-king alliance that carried Lot away out of Sodom (Gen 14:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Arioch; in sacred history he is captain of the guard to Nebuchadnezzar, and also a king of Ellasar in the days of Abram.
webster_full: ARIOCH, n. Lion-like; a proper name in the Hebrew Scriptures.
The captain of the king's guard under Nebuchadnezzar, charged to destroy the wise men.
To him Daniel answered with counsel and wisdom, and obtained a delay.
He brought Daniel in haste before the king to declare the interpretation.
Also, Arioch king of Ellasar, one of the four kings who warred against the cities of the plain.
scriptures: Dan 2:14
Then Daniel answered with counsel and wisdom to Arioch the captain of the king's guard, which was gone forth to slay the wise men of Babylon:
Dan 2:15
He answered and said to Arioch the king's captain, Why is the decree so hasty from the king? Then Arioch made the thing known to Daniel.
Dan 2:24

Therefore Daniel went in unto Arioch, whom the king had ordained to destroy the wise men of Babylon: he went and said thus unto him; Destroy not the wise men of Babylon: bring me in before the king, and I will shew unto the king the interpretation.
Gen 14:1
And it came to pass in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations;
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is the wisdom of the believer under an unjust decree: not defiance and not despair, but a discreet question and a request for time in which God may answer.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Arioch is a Babylonian officer and nobody has contested him. What the encounter sets against the modern instinct is Daniel's manner. A death squad is at the door on the authority of a tyrant's bad night, and the young man neither denounces the king nor bribes the captain nor flees. He answers with prudence, asks why, and requests an interval. The interval he uses for prayer: he goes to his three companions that they might desire mercies of the God of heaven concerning this secret.

The principle to recover is that faith under pressure is usually quiet and always dependent. Scripture praises “A soft answer turneth away wrath” (Pro 15:1), and Christ sent out His own with the same doubleness: “be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves” (Mat 10:16). Daniel's courage in chapter 6 is celebrated because he would not stop praying; his wisdom in chapter 2 is that he knew when to ask a captain a civil question. Both are obedience, and the church that can only manage the loud kind will lose men it might have kept.

Hebrew tabbach (H2877) — executioner, guardsman; his office was literally chief slaughterer.
Aramaic 'eta' (H5843) — counsel; the first half of Daniel's answer.
Aramaic te'em (H2942) — taste, discretion, decree; the second half, and the king's decree also.
Aramaic raz (H7328) — secret; the word for the dream God revealed.
usage: “Arioch the captain of the king's guard” — the man sent to kill, met with a question.
“Why is the decree so hasty from the king?” — prudence buying an hour for prayer.
“Then Arioch brought in Daniel before the king in haste” — the courtier at his most useful.

pos: n. (a Persian title of office, rendered in the Authorized Version as the style of the governor of Judah under the great king — borne by Zerubbabel and by Nehemiah)
etymology: A Persian loan-word taken into Hebrew as Tirshatha, generally derived from an Old Persian root meaning to be feared or revered — hence his excellency. It is not a name but a style, always written with the article: the Tirshatha.
biblical_def: Tirshatha is one of the handful of foreign administrative words the Authorized Version carries over untranslated, and it marks a precise historical situation: Judah after the captivity was not a kingdom but a province, and the man over it held his commission from a Gentile emperor. The title first appears in the register of the returned: “And the Tirshatha said unto them, that they should not eat of the most holy things, till there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim” (Ezr 2:63). That is a governor ruling on a question of ceremonial purity — certain families could not prove their priestly descent, and the Tirshatha suspended their privileges rather than presume. Nehemiah is named with the title outright: “And Nehemiah, which is the Tirshatha, and Ezra the priest the scribe, and the Levites that taught the people, said unto all the people, This day is holy unto the LORD your God” (Neh 8:9), and he signs the covenant at its head, “Nehemiah, the Tirshatha, the son of Hachaliah” (Neh 10:1). The office is real civil authority: he levied nothing for himself, he rebuilt a wall, he enforced the sabbath at the gates. But it is authority held under Artaxerxes, and the word itself is a Persian word. Every time the Chronicler writes Tirshatha instead of king, he is confessing that the throne of David stood empty and that the people were still, in the words of Nehemiah's own prayer, servants in the land God gave their fathers.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Tirshatha; it is the Persian title of the governor of Judah after the captivity, borne by Zerubbabel and by Nehemiah.
webster_full: TIRSHATHA, n. A title of office, of Persian original, signifying one to be revered; his excellency.
The style of the governor of Judea under the kings of Persia, always used with the article.
The Tirshatha ordered that those who could not prove their priestly descent should not eat of the most holy things.
Nehemiah the son of Hachaliah is expressly called the Tirshatha.
The word marks the province, not the kingdom; Judah had a governor where it once had a king.
scriptures: Ezr 2:63
And the Tirshatha said unto them, that they should not eat of the most holy things, till there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim.
Neh 8:9
And Nehemiah, which is the Tirshatha, and Ezra the priest the scribe, and the Levites that taught the people, said unto all the people, This day is holy unto the LORD your God; mourn not, nor weep.
Neh 10:1
Now those that sealed were, Nehemiah, the Tirshatha, the son of Hachaliah, and Zidkijah,
Neh 7:65
And the Tirshatha said unto them, that they should not eat of the most holy things, till there stood up a priest with Urim and Thummim.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this title. The principle to recover is that God's people have often lived under a legitimate civil authority that is not their own, and that faithfulness in such a season is neither revolt nor assimilation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Tirshatha is an archaic loan-word and nobody has contested it. What it sets against the present moment is the posture of the restoration community. Judah was governed by a Persian appointee under Persian law, paid Persian tribute, and rebuilt its wall by Persian permit — and Nehemiah neither pretended the empire was the kingdom of God nor treated his office as a compromise too dirty to hold. He took the commission, wept over the ruins, prayed to the God of heaven before he answered the king, and used a pagan power's authority to restore the worship of the true God.

The principle to recover is the ordinary Christian doctrine of the civil sphere. The magistrate is God's minister whether he knows it or not (Rom 13:4); Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the peace of the city; Daniel served three dynasties without eating their meat. What a believer under such an authority may not do is either of the two easy things — conclude that because the state is not Christian nothing may be done through it, or conclude that because something may be done through it the state has become the kingdom. Nehemiah signed himself the Tirshatha and kept praying for the throne of David.

usage: “And the Tirshatha said unto them” — a civil governor ruling on the holy things.
“Nehemiah, which is the Tirshatha” — the title attached to the man by name.
“Till there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim” — an honest confession of what was missing.

pos: n. (the servant of Elisha, who ran after Naaman for money and garments and was struck with the leper's leprosy for it)
etymology: From Hebrew Gechazi, commonly explained as valley of vision or, following another derivation, denier — a name the narrative makes bitterly apt, since his ruin turned on a lie told to a prophet's face.
biblical_def: Gehazi is Elisha's body-servant through the great cycle of the prophet's ministry, and he is not introduced as a villain. He announces the Shunammite's childlessness and so occasions the promise of her son (2Ki 4:14-16); he is sent running ahead with the prophet's staff when the boy dies; he is standing there when Naaman the Syrian comes down with his horses and chariots. Elisha refuses the Syrian's gift absolutely: “As the LORD liveth, before whom I stand, I will receive none” (2Ki 5:16). What his servant thought of that refusal is recorded word for word: “my master hath spared Naaman this Syrian, in not receiving at his hands that which he brought: but, as the LORD liveth, I will run after him, and take somewhat of him” (2Ki 5:20). He swears by the LORD's life in the act of resolving to lie, invents two young men of the sons of the prophets who need “a talent of silver, and two changes of garments”, hides the spoil, and presents himself for orders. Elisha's question is unanswerable: “Went not mine heart with thee, when the man turned again from his chariot to meet thee? Is it a time to receive money, and to receive garments” (2Ki 5:26). The sentence is exact retribution: “The leprosy therefore of Naaman shall cleave unto thee, and unto thy seed for ever. And he went out from his presence a leper as white as snow” (2Ki 5:27). He appears once afterward, telling the king of Israel the great things Elisha had done (2Ki 8:4), which suggests the man lived on in the outer circle of a ministry he could no longer touch.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Gehazi; in sacred history he is the servant of Elisha, smitten with leprosy for taking by fraud the reward his master refused.
webster_full: GEHAZI, n. A proper name; the servant and attendant of the prophet Elisha.
He waited on the prophet through the history of the Shunammite and her son.
When Elisha refused the gift of Naaman, Gehazi ran after the Syrian and obtained silver and raiment by a lie.
For this covetousness the leprosy of Naaman was pronounced upon him and upon his seed.
He went out from the prophet's presence a leper as white as snow.
scriptures: But he said, As the LORD liveth, before whom I stand, I will receive none. And he urged him to take it; but he refused.

But Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said, Behold, my master hath spared Naaman this Syrian, in not receiving at his hands that which he brought: but, as the LORD liveth, I will run after him, and take somewhat of him.

And he said unto him, Went not mine heart with thee, when the man turned again from his chariot to meet thee? Is it a time to receive money, and to receive garments, and oliveyards, and vineyards, and sheep, and oxen, and menservants, and maidservants?
The leprosy therefore of Naaman shall cleave unto thee, and unto thy seed for ever. And he went out from his presence a leper as white as snow.
corruption_summary: Gehazi is treated in modern retellings as a sympathetic figure who wanted his share, and the money is read as the small sin in a story about healing. Scripture treats the traffic in God's free gifts as the sin that made a leper of a prophet's servant, and the New Testament names the same crime twice more.
corruption_paragraphs: The soft reading of Gehazi runs like this: Elisha was austere, Naaman could easily afford it, the servant had served long and got nothing, and the punishment does not fit the crime. Every part of that is a refusal to see what happened. Naaman had just confessed, “Behold, now I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel” (2Ki 5:15). Elisha refused payment so that the Syrian would carry home an unpurchasable mercy. Gehazi ran after him and sold it, for a talent of silver and two suits of clothes, and in doing so told a new convert that the God of Israel had a price after all. He did not steal money; he corrupted a testimony.

The New Testament names the sin without euphemism. Peter to Simon the sorcerer: “Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money” (Act 8:20). Paul of the false teachers in Crete, who subvert whole houses “for filthy lucre&#39;s sake” (Tit 1:11). Peter again of the men who “through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise of you” (2Pe 2:3). The modern prosperity preacher, the healing evangelist with a donation line, the ministry that meters access to prayer by the size of the gift — these are not new phenomena to be assessed on their fruits. They are Gehazi running down the road after the chariot, and the sentence on them is already written.

pos: n. (a name borne by many men in Israel — a Levite singer of David's choir, a treasurer of the house of God, a son of Jehoshaphat, and an overseer under Hezekiah)
etymology: From Hebrew Yechi'el, God liveth or may God live, from chayah, to live, and El, God. The Authorized Version also spells it Jehieli for the family (1Ch 26:21) and once Jeiel.
biblical_def: Jehiel is one of those Old Testament names carried by so many men that the Chronicler has to identify each by his father or his post, and the effect of reading them together is a picture of the whole apparatus of ordered worship. There is Jehiel the Levite, set with the harps when the ark came up to Jerusalem, listed among “their brethren of the second degree” who were “the porters” (1Ch 15:18). There is Jehiel the Gershonite over the treasures of the house of the LORD (1Ch 29:8). There is Jehiel among “the sons of Jehoshaphat” (2Ch 21:2), murdered with his brothers when Jehoram secured his throne. There is Jehiel one of the overseers under Hezekiah's reform: “were overseers under the hand of Cononiah and Shimei his brother, at the commandment of Hezekiah the king” (2Ch 31:13). And there is the Jehiel whose son Shechaniah spoke the first honest word in Ezra's reform of the strange marriages: “We have trespassed against our God, and have taken strange wives of the people of the land: yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing” (Ezr 10:2). Five centuries and five men, and the name means God liveth every time. That is what a covenant people does with a name: it keeps confessing the same thing in every generation, whether the man who bears it plays a psaltery, counts tithes, or dies at his brother's hand.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Jehiel; in sacred history it is the name of several Levites, treasurers and princes, signifying God liveth.
webster_full: JEHIEL, n. God liveth; a proper name borne by many men in the Hebrew Scriptures.
A Levite of the second degree, appointed with instruments of musick when the ark was brought up.
A Gershonite set over the treasures of the house of God in the days of David.
A son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, slain by his brother Jehoram.
An overseer of the offerings and tithes under Hezekiah, and the father of Shechaniah in the days of Ezra.

And he had brethren the sons of Jehoshaphat, Azariah, and Jehiel, and Zechariah, and Azariah, and Michael, and Shephatiah: all these were the sons of Jehoshaphat king of Israel.

And Jehiel, and Azaziah, and Nahath, and Asahel, and Jerimoth, and Jozabad, and Eliel, and Ismachiah, and Mahath, and Benaiah, were overseers under the hand of Cononiah and Shimei his brother, at the commandment of Hezekiah the king, and Azariah the ruler of the house of God.
Ezr 10:2

And Shechaniah the son of Jehiel, one of the sons of Elam, answered and said unto Ezra, We have trespassed against our God, and have taken strange wives of the people of the land: yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that the ordinary, repeated, unremarkable names of the covenant people are themselves a confession, and that God keeps books on men the world never noticed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Jehiel is a name in genealogies and nobody has contested it. What the crowd of Jehiels sets against the modern reader is the habit of skipping the lists. The Chronicler wrote them on purpose. He is answering a returned remnant who wondered whether their own small service in a small province mattered, and his answer is a register: here are the men who carried, sang, counted, guarded and swept, named and dated, because the LORD does not lose the names of His servants.

The principle to recover is the dignity of the unremembered. Malachi promises that “a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name” (Mal 3:16), and the Lord tells the seventy to rejoice rather “because your names are written in heaven” (Luk 10:20). A church that measures a life by platform and audience has forgotten what the genealogies are for. Five men named God liveth, none of them famous, all of them written down.

pos: n. (a fisherman of Galilee, husband of Salome and father of the apostles James and John, left in the ship with the hired servants when his sons were called)
etymology: Greek Zebedaios, from Hebrew Zabdi or Zebadyah, the LORD hath given or gift of the LORD, from zabad, to bestow. The name is a confession, and the man was asked to give back exactly what the name says he had received.
biblical_def: Zebedee is named eleven times in the Gospels and speaks not once. He is a Galilean fisherman of some substance — his boat carried hired servants as well as family — and he was at work with his sons when Christ came along the shore: “he saw other two brethren, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them” (Mat 4:21). The next verse is the whole of the man's trial in eleven words: “And they immediately left the ship and their father, and followed him” (Mat 4:22). Mark adds the detail that softens nothing: “they left their father Zebedee in the ship with the hired servants, and went after him” (Mar 1:20). Luke shows the family was in partnership with Simon (Luk 5:10), so a going business lost half its young men in an afternoon. His wife Salome followed Christ, ministered to Him of her substance, came asking for thrones for her boys (Mat 20:20), and stood at the cross. His sons became the Sons of Thunder (Mar 3:17), and one of them was the first apostle martyred (Act 12:2) while the other outlived them all. Of Zebedee himself, Scripture records the nets, the hired servants, and the silence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Zebedee; in sacred history he is a fisherman of Galilee, the father of the apostles James and John.
webster_full: ZEBEDEE, n. The gift of the LORD; a proper name in the Greek Scriptures.
A fisherman of Galilee, the husband of Salome and father of James and John.
He was mending his nets in the ship when our Saviour called his two sons.
His trade employed hired servants, and was in partnership with Simon Peter.
He is named often as the father, but no word of his is recorded.
scriptures: Mat 4:21
And going on from thence, he saw other two brethren, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them.
Mat 4:22
And they immediately left the ship and their father, and followed him.
Mar 1:20
And straightway he called them: and they left their father Zebedee in the ship with the hired servants, and went after him.
And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, come unto him, saying, Master, we would that thou shouldest do for us whatsoever we shall desire.
corruption_summary: Modern devotional writing turns Zebedee into a study in the emotional cost of ministry to families. The Gospels present the call of his sons as the absolute claim of Christ, which is a harder thing and a better one.
corruption_paragraphs: It is now common to read Mark 1:20 through the lens of family systems — the father abandoned, the business disrupted, the unprocessed grief of the man left in the boat. The instinct is not entirely wrong; Scripture never pretends discipleship is costless, and Zebedee is put in the text precisely so the reader feels the weight of the two sons walking away. But the therapeutic frame changes the subject. Mark is not describing a family crisis; he is describing what happens when the Son of God calls a man, and the hired servants are mentioned to show the reader that Christ's claim does not wait on a succession plan.

The Lord said it plainly enough: “He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Mat 10:37), and He also said, promising the return, that no man has left house or brethren or father for His sake “But he shall receive an hundredfold now in this time” (Mar 10:30). Both stand. The fifth commandment is not repealed by the call — John took the mother of Jesus into his own home at the cross, which is a son honouring a parent while hanging on for the kingdom. What the frame of trauma cannot supply is the accounting Christ Himself gives: the boat was worth losing.

pos: n. (a chief of the porters of the house of the LORD, whose family kept the gates from the days of David to the days of Nehemiah)
etymology: From Hebrew Talmon, of uncertain derivation, connected by some with telem, a furrow, and by others with a root meaning oppressed. The name attaches to a house rather than to a single life: the children of Talmon return in the register of the captivity centuries after the man.
biblical_def: Talmon is named among the porters — the gatekeepers of the sanctuary, an office the Chronicler treats with the seriousness of the priesthood itself. “And the porters were, Shallum, and Akkub, and Talmon, and Ahiman, and their brethren: Shallum was the chief” (1Ch 9:17). The work was not ornamental. The porters lodged round about the house of God, opened it every morning, kept the chambers and the treasuries, counted the vessels in and out, and had charge of who came through the gate — because Scripture is emphatic that not everyone might come in, and no unclean thing was to enter. When the captivity ended, the list of those who came up includes the doorkeepers by household: “The children of the porters: the children of Shallum, the children of Ater, the children of Talmon” (Ezr 2:42). They are still there when the wall is finished: “Moreover the porters, Akkub, Talmon, and their brethren that kept the gates, were an hundred seventy and two” (Neh 11:19), and again in Nehemiah's roll of the ministers, “were porters keeping the ward at the thresholds of the gates” (Neh 12:25). A family of doorkeepers, faithful across five hundred years and two temples, who never preached a sermon or sang a psalm and without whom the house would have stood open to anything.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Talmon; in sacred history he is a chief of the porters, or doorkeepers, of the house of the LORD.
webster_full: TALMON, n. A proper name in the Hebrew Scriptures; a Levite of the order of the porters.
The porters kept the gates of the house of God and lodged round about it.
They had the oversight of the chambers, the treasuries and the holy vessels.
The children of Talmon returned from the captivity with Zerubbabel.
In the days of Nehemiah the porters that kept the gates were an hundred seventy and two.
scriptures: And the porters were, Shallum, and Akkub, and Talmon, and Ahiman, and their brethren: Shallum was the chief;
Ezr 2:42

The children of the porters: the children of Shallum, the children of Ater, the children of Talmon, the children of Akkub, the children of Hatita, the children of Shobai, in all an hundred thirty and nine.
Moreover the porters, Akkub, Talmon, and their brethren that kept the gates, were an hundred seventy and two.
Mattaniah, and Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, Akkub, were porters keeping the ward at the thresholds of the gates.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that guarding the door of God's house is a ministry, that some things must be kept out, and that the man at the threshold is doing holy work.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Talmon is a doorkeeper in a list and nobody has contested him. What his office sets against the present church is the whole idea of a threshold. The porters existed because the house of the LORD had a boundary; there were courts the uncircumcised did not enter, vessels the unconsecrated did not touch, and days on which the gate stayed shut. To keep the ward was to say no at the right times, and the Chronicler counts the men who did it and writes down their names.

The principle to recover is the discipline of the visible church. Christ committed keys to His church (Mat 16:19; Mat 18:17-18), and the Supper is fenced: “he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself” (1Co 11:29). A congregation that has no porters — no membership, no examination, no elders willing to stand at the threshold — has not become more loving; it has abolished an office God appointed and left the treasuries unwatched. And the honour of the work is settled by the psalm: “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness” (Psa 84:10).
